statement: The linearization of a differentiable function f at a point a is the first-order Taylor expansion of f about a, i.e. the tangent line/plane L_a(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) (scalar case) or f(x) ≈ f(p) + ∇f|_p · (x-p) (vector case), used to approximate f near a/p.

symbols.meaning: linearization of f at x = a
slope used in the point-slope line equation, set equal to f'(a)
derivative (slope of tangent line) of f evaluated at a
linearization point for a two-variable function f(x,y)
linearization point for a multivariable function f(x)

steps.text: Linearization is defined as approximating y = f(x) near x = a by the first-order Taylor expansion of f around a, requiring the basic condition L_a(a) = f(a).
Start from the point-slope form of a line through (H,K) with slope M: y - K = M(x - H).
Substitute the point (H,K) = (a, f(a)) to get L_a(x): y = f(a) + M(x - a).
Because a differentiable function is locally linear, choose M to be the slope of the line tangent to f at x = a, i.e. M = f'(a).
Substituting M = f'(a) gives the linearization of f at x = a: y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a).

Extend to a two-variable function f(x,y) at p(a,b) by adding one first-order term per variable, each a partial derivative evaluated at p times the corresponding displacement: f(x,y) ≈ f(a,b) + ∂f/∂x|_{a,b}(x-a) + ∂f/∂y|_{a,b}(y-b).
Generalize to an n-variable function f(x) at point p by packaging the partial derivatives into the gradient and the displacement terms into a dot product: f(x) ≈ f(p) + ∇f|_p · (x - p).

Apply the same first-order expansion to the right-hand side of a dynamical system dx/dt = F(x,t) at a point of interest x0, replacing the gradient with the x-Jacobian DF(x0,t) of the vector field F: dx/dt ≈ F(x0,t) + DF(x0,t)·(x - x0).

assumptions.assumption: f(x) is differentiable on an interval containing a and b (the evaluation point and the linearization point).
assumptions.breaks_when: f is not differentiable at or near the linearization point, so no tangent line/plane (no f'(a) or ∇f|_p) exists.

assumptions.assumption: a (or x, or p) is close to the linearization point.
assumptions.breaks_when: The evaluation point is far from the linearization point, so the first-order term no longer approximates f well.

failure_modes.signature: y computed from L_a(x) (or the multivariable/vector version) diverges noticeably from the true f(x) as x moves away from a/p.
failure_modes.cause: Higher-order Taylor terms, which the linearization discards, become non-negligible as |x - a| increases.

failure_modes.mode: Linearization is undefined at the chosen point.
failure_modes.signature: f'(a), the partial derivatives, or ∇f|_p cannot be computed (do not exist) at the point of interest.
failure_modes.cause: f is not differentiable at that point, so there is no tangent line/plane to serve as the linearization.
